值得閱讀的理由

  • 深刻剖析西班牙87歲老婦人因租約糾紛遭強制驅逐並離世的悲劇，探討居住正義與法律邊界。
  • 解析西班牙「舊租約」歷史背景與法規變革，了解長期低於市價租約引發的地主與租客衝突。
  • 全面拆解西班牙住房危機的三大核心成因：薪資停滯與高房價失衡、社會住宅短缺，以及觀光資本排擠效應。

摘要

八旬老婦遭驅離逝世引爆全國怒火

作者指出，西班牙馬德里一位87歲的老婦人瑪麗．卡門（Mari Carmen）在同一間公寓生活了長達70年且按時繳租，卻因法規修改面臨強制遷離。歷經多年訴訟與抗爭後，她在第四次驅逐行動中被擔架抬上救護車送醫，不久後在醫院過世。這場悲劇引爆西班牙全國性的強烈抗議，抗議者佔領太陽門廣場要求政府立法禁止在無安置方案下驅逐房客，更促使首相解散國會提前大選。

歷史遺留的「舊租約」與法律角力

作者回溯源頭，瑪麗．卡門自1956年佛朗哥獨裁時期便與父母入住，合約屬於早期受法律保障、租金極低且可世代繼承的「舊租約」。然而，1994年西班牙修法限制繼承次數與期限。當公寓產權於近年轉賣給不動產公司後，新房東要求調漲至她無法負擔的租金並提起訴訟。法院最終判定繼承期限已過而判房東勝訴，儘管各方在悲劇發生前夕曾達成協議讓她以原本租金重返公寓，但她已來不及回家。

薪資停滯與房市供需嚴重失衡

作者進一步探討民眾憤怒背後的深層住房危機。首先是薪資完全追不上房價，過去十年間工資僅成長30%，房價與租金漲幅卻高達80%以上，單身租客租金甚至吃掉過半收入；其次是供給嚴重不足，2008年金融海嘯後營建業萎縮，加上社會住宅比例僅佔約1.5%至1.7%，遠低於歐盟平均，預估至2028年將面臨高達百萬戶的住宅缺口。

外資觀光熱潮加劇居住困境

最後，作者提到外資湧入與過度觀光帶來的排擠效應。大量海外人口湧入使需求激增，房東紛紛將長租轉為利潤豐厚的高價短租或觀光用房，甚至在旅遊旺季驅趕本地租客。目前全西班牙仍有約3,000處位於黃金地段的「舊租約」房產，租金僅為市價的一小部分。這類歷史制度與當前市場機制的劇烈摩擦，讓西班牙陷入了嚴峻的居住危機。

The. grandmother was eventually carried out. on a stretcher to an ambulance and. taken to the hospital, where she passed. away shortly after, never being able to. return to the home she had lived in for. most of her life. What exactly did the. grandmother do wrong? Actually, nothing. at all. The problem stemmed from a. lease her father signed 70 years ago,. combined with subsequent revisions to. rental laws. What was initially just a. legal dispute between a landlord and a. tenant unexpectedly ignited outrage. across all of Spain. Large crowds took. to the streets to seek justice for the. grandmother, demanding that the. government protect the right to housing. , while parliament argued intensely. over housing policy, eventually leading. the Prime Minister to dissolve. parliament and call for early elections. . The then 17-year-old Mari Carmen moved. into an apartment in Madrid with her. parents. Her father passed away in 1960. , and the lease was transferred to her. mother. In 2005, her mother also passed. away, and the lease was then inherited. by Mari Carmen. This system is known as. the "old lease," and it has several.

specific characteristics. Simply put,. these were rental contracts protected. by law in the early days; not only was. the rent far below market rates, but. under certain conditions, family. members could inherit the lease, and. landlords could not refuse. According. to BBC, the rent Mari Carmen inherited. was 500 euros, which is nearly 18,000. New Taiwan Dollars at the current. exchange rate, while her monthly. pension was 1,350 euros, or about. 48,000 New Taiwan Dollars, which was. initially affordable. The problem arose. in 2018 when the owner's family sold. the entire building to a real estate. company. The company offered to sell. the apartment to Mari Carmen for 8.8. million New Taiwan Dollars and asked if. she wanted to buy it. However, the. elderly lady was too old to obtain a. mortgage, and she had no relatives to. act as guarantors. Later, the company. sold the apartment to another real. estate firm. This company initially. demanded rent......that was nearly. double her pension. They later offered. a discount, but it was still 300 euros. higher than her monthly pension, which. is nearly 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars; even if she didn't eat or drink, she. still couldn't afford it. Then, in 2020. , the company filed a lawsuit, claiming. that the old lease Mari Carmen. inherited was no longer valid. This. brings us to the Spanish rental law. amended in 1994. Previously, old rental. contracts could be passed down through. generations, but the new law began. limiting the number of successions and. their duration. Like Maria Carmen,. whose father passed the lease to her. mother, and then her mother passed it.

to her, this represents a second. succession. Under current regulations,. an adult child like her can generally. only remain for two more years. The. legal battle then began. The initial. 2022 court ruling actually found in. Maria Carmen’s favor, reasoning that. since she had rented for so many years,. the landlord could not suddenly renege. on the agreement. However, the landlord. refused to accept this and appealed. The second-instance court ruled that. even if the landlord had continued to. collect rent for years, it did not. override the legal time limits on old. contracts, thus overturning the verdict. in favor of the landlord. Later, the. Supreme Court did not accept Maria. Carmen’s appeal, and the ruling. became final. During these years of. litigation, tenant unions and neighbors. joined in to help. Over the past year,. three eviction attempts were delayed. due to protests, but on September 23rd. of this year, the fourth eviction. finally arrived. Large crowds gathered. outside the apartment that day; police. cordoned off the area while court. officials entered to carry out the. eviction. The elderly woman, whose. health had deteriorated, was carried to. an ambulance on a stretcher by. paramedics. This scene spread across. Spain via television and the internet,. causing a national outcry, as many. citizens felt deeply for the elderly. woman’s plight. The situation drew. immense sympathy. Following the. eviction, hundreds of people. spontaneously went to Madrid's landmark. "Puerta del Sol" that weekend to set up. tents, demanding the government pass a. "Maria Carmen Law" to ban evictions.

without providing alternative housing,. and tents began to spring up everywhere. , spreading rapidly. It escalated. quickly. The reason people are this. angry is that Spain’s housing crisis. is becoming increasingly severe. There. are several problems; first, wages. cannot keep up with housing prices. During the 2008 financial crisis, Spain. experienced a property bubble burst and. skyrocketing unemployment. Despite the. later economic recovery, salaries have. completely failed to keep pace with. soaring housing costs. According to El. País statistics, over the decade from. 2015 to 2025, Spanish wages grew by. only 30%, while the cost of home. purchases rose by 80%and rents surged. by 87%. Idealista points out that in. the second quarter of 2025, an average. household needed to spend 39%of their. after-tax income to rent a two-bedroom. home; single tenants are even worse off. , with rent likely consuming over half. their salary. Additionally, Spain’s. unemployment rate remains chronically. high; although the second quarter of. this year saw the lowest level since. the financial crisis, it is still. nearing 10%. Furthermore, the economy. is overly reliant on low-wage tourism. and service industries, leaving the. working class helpless against high. housing prices. Second, there is a. severe shortage of housing supply. Before the market crash, Spain could. build 600,000 new homes a year. However. , the construction sector was severely. crippled after the crash, and it is. estimated that only 91,000 homes will. be completed by 2025. More critically,. social housing in Spain accounts for. only 1.5%to 1.7%of the total, far below.

the EU average of 6%to 7%. This is. because past policies over-encouraged. home ownership, with most units sold. off directly rather than kept for. long-term government rentals. Plus,. with little profit to be made,. developers simply didn't want to build. them. Furthermore, Spain has 17. autonomous communities, and central. government policies often stall due to. political tug-of-wars with regional. governments, leading to stagnant. construction. The government estimates. that by 2028, the national housing. shortage will reach as high as one. million units. Third, the crowding-out. effect of foreign capital and tourists. Since 2015, Spain’s population has. surged by over 3 million, mostly. overseas individuals flooding into. major cities like Madrid and Barcelona. Demand has skyrocketed, but supply. remains stagnant. The massive tourism. industry has created two major issues:. first, landlords have converted. long-term rentals into more profitable. short-term tourist rentals, drastically. reducing space for residents. Second,. the influx of hot foreign money has. driven up prices, so home values in. popular areas are no longer determined. by local wages. Taking Galicia in the. northwest as an example, many landlords. , eager for summer tourist profits,. only sign seasonal leases, kicking. tenants out when summer arrives to rent. to tourists. This twisted ecosystem is. ruthlessly stripping local residents of. their basic right to housing. The. accumulation of these problems has led. to a situation where, although 73%of. Spaniards own their homes, over 60%of. young people aged 18 to 34 still live.

with their parents. Back to the case of. Mari Carmen. On September 28th, with. mediation from the Madrid city. government, both parties reached an. agreement to sign a new eight-year. lease. The grandmother could move back. into her original apartment, with rent. capped at no more than 30%of her. monthly income, which is about 500. euros, similar to what she paid before. Prime Minister Sánchez also urgently. proposed housing reforms, hoping to. limit rent increases and strengthen. tenant protections, but two housing. bills were rejected by parliament in. succession. Sánchez simply announced. the dissolution of parliament on. October 6th and moved the general. election forward to November 29th,. letting voters directly decide the. future of Spain's housing policy. Unexpectedly, while all parties were in. chaos, Mari Carmen passed away in the. hospital on October 7th, never making. it home. Speaking of this, let's put. ourselves in their shoes: if you were. the landlord, would you continue to. rent to Mari Carmen at a low price? The. apartment she rents is located here, in. an upscale residential area of Madrid. It's next to the famous Retiro Park,. with the Prado Museum to the west and. Atocha Station just a bit further south. —the amenities and environment are. excellent. This apartment is about 28. square meters. Based on average listing. prices from rental websites, Maria. Carmen is renting this prime property. for less than a fraction of the market. rate. Currently, there are still about. 3,000 such old rental properties left. in all of Spain, mostly located in the. city centers of Madrid and Barcelona.

Although the terms of each contract. vary, generally speaking, the rent is. usually only one-fifth of the market. price, and in some cases, it's as low. as one-tenth. While this lease is. certainly a great deal for the tenant,. if you're the landlord, you're in big. trouble. Terminating this type of lease. is a very complex process. But if you. keep renting it out, the rent you. collect likely won't even cover the. costs of ownership, such as taxes,. maintenance, and management fees,. making it a financial burden instead. This situation makes me reflect; Taiwan. officially became a super-aged society. last year. With our high housing prices. , many people simply cannot afford to. buy a home and have to rent. indefinitely. The question is, when. these people grow old and retire, will. landlords still be willing to rent to. them? Taiwan's current Housing Act. already includes seniors over 65 as a. target group for social housing, but. being eligible to apply doesn't. necessarily mean there will be a home. available for them. The Maria Carmen. case reminds us that housing policy. shouldn't just focus on how to make. homes affordable for young people; we. must also consider what those who will. never be able to afford a home will do. when they get old. 摘要

惡魔即將回歸：金槿植案引發南韓社會集體焦慮

作者指出，南韓近期因重大兒少性侵犯金槿植即將刑滿獲釋，引發廣大家長與社區居民的極度恐慌。金槿植曾於2006年間誘拐並性侵11名未成年人，年紀最小的被害人僅9歲。原定於2022年出獄的他，因檢方即時查出其於2002年的懸案並涉及獄中施暴，獲法院追加刑期延至2027年釋放。然而，法院駁回了檢方對其施以化學去勢的聲請，僅命其配戴電子腳鐐十年，使大眾深感不安，深怕這顆「定時炸彈」再次危害社區。

借鑑美國經驗：南韓版「潔西卡法」重回輿論焦點

面對大眾恐慌，南韓再度激起制定「潔西卡法案」（Jessica\'s Law）的呼聲。作者說明，該法源於美國佛州一名九歲女童潔西卡遭三級性侵累犯殺害的慘劇，促使美國各州立法嚴格限制性侵犯出獄後的居住範圍。南韓雖然設有性犯罪者資訊公開系統，但過往如趙斗淳、朴炳化等連環性侵犯出獄後租屋於校園或住宅區附近，屢次引爆住戶抗議與恐慌。南韓法務部因此提出《高風險性犯罪者指定居住法案》，擬強制將高風險性侵犯集中安置於國家設立的隔離設施中。

安全與人權的拉鋸：指定居住法案的爭議與流局

法案提出後引發各界正反激辯。贊成方主張，高風險性犯罪者的再犯率高，保護兒少安全是國家的底線，現行電子腳鐐防不勝防，必須透過集中管理與性衝動抑制治療來防範再犯。反對方則質疑，服刑完畢後強制收容有違憲與雙重處罰之嫌，嚴重侵犯居住遷徙自由；且設施選址面臨嚴重的鄰避效應（NIMBY），若長期全面隔離，恐讓受刑人更趨反社會，治標不治本。這項法案最終因違憲爭議與地方抗拒，於2024年5月國會任期結束時自動廢案。

制度的借鏡與反思：密集監管代替絕對隔離

作者最後借鏡台灣現況指出，台灣與南韓同樣面臨人口稠密的問題，若對更生人施加極端的生活空間限制，往往會將其逼入絕境，因無法謀生或憤恨而更容易重蹈覆轍。因此，台灣的《性侵害犯罪防治法》目前採取密集監控與身心治療輔導，而非採取絕對的空間隔離設施，試圖在防範犯罪再發與維持社會復歸機能之間尋求務實的平衡。

惡魔即將回歸：金槿植案引發南韓社會集體焦慮

作者指出，南韓近期因重大兒少性侵犯金槿植即將刑滿獲釋，引發廣大家長與社區居民的極度恐慌。金槿植曾於2006年間誘拐並性侵11名未成年人，年紀最小的被害人僅9歲。原定於2022年出獄的他，因檢方即時查出其於2002年的懸案並涉及獄中施暴，獲法院追加刑期延至2027年釋放。然而，法院駁回了檢方對其施以化學去勢的聲請，僅命其配戴電子腳鐐十年，使大眾深感不安，深怕這顆「定時炸彈」再次危害社區。

借鑑美國經驗：南韓版「潔西卡法」重回輿論焦點

面對大眾恐慌，南韓再度激起制定「潔西卡法案」（Jessica\'s Law）的呼聲。作者說明，該法源於美國佛州一名九歲女童潔西卡遭三級性侵累犯殺害的慘劇，促使美國各州立法嚴格限制性侵犯出獄後的居住範圍。南韓雖然設有性犯罪者資訊公開系統，但過往如趙斗淳、朴炳化等連環性侵犯出獄後租屋於校園或住宅區附近，屢次引爆住戶抗議與恐慌。南韓法務部因此提出《高風險性犯罪者指定居住法案》，擬強制將高風險性侵犯集中安置於國家設立的隔離設施中。

安全與人權的拉鋸：指定居住法案的爭議與流局

法案提出後引發各界正反激辯。贊成方主張，高風險性犯罪者的再犯率高，保護兒少安全是國家的底線，現行電子腳鐐防不勝防，必須透過集中管理與性衝動抑制治療來防範再犯。反對方則質疑，服刑完畢後強制收容有違憲與雙重處罰之嫌，嚴重侵犯居住遷徙自由；且設施選址面臨嚴重的鄰避效應（NIMBY），若長期全面隔離，恐讓受刑人更趨反社會，治標不治本。這項法案最終因違憲爭議與地方抗拒，於2024年5月國會任期結束時自動廢案。
